title: Callum and the Clockwork Heart
markdown:
Callum’s mind ran like good clockwork: wheels in the right order, no wasted tick. Fern the hedgehog, usually as lively as a tumble of acorns, lay still in her mossy bed. Tiny shallow breaths barely stirred her spines. A drowsy sickness had settled, and Callum’s own chest felt heavier for it.

He offered a juicy berry. She barely twitched. He tucked a warm leaf around her. She stayed listless. This was more than a nap, and he was not in the business of pretending it was.

He hurried to Dr. Ada Brook, whose lab was a cheerful chaos of bubbling beakers and spinning gears, spectacles perched as if they had a sense of humour. “Fern is so sleepy,” he said, which was accurate and also not enough.

Dr. Ada adjusted the spectacles. “More than sleepiness. Her body needs oxygen the way a tiny engine needs fuel. The delivery has slowed.”

“Delivery,” Callum said. “Like a postman?” He pictured, briefly and against his will, a hedgehog in a very small hat.

Dr. Ada’s chuckle sounded like rattling teacups. “In a way. This postman travels inside. Heart and blood, working together, carrying oxygen from toes to twitching ears. Fern’s heart is not pumping that cargo strongly enough.”

She led him to a gleaming clockwork heart no bigger than a teacup, clear tubes branching like tiny roots. Tick-tock, tick-tock. A controlled pump sent bright red liquid — oxygen-rich blood, for the sake of the lesson — through the tubes. “Everywhere. Brain. Fingers. Toes. The bits too small to have opinions.”

Fern, nestled weakly in Callum’s arms, peeked and gave a faint hopeful squeak. She felt a strange tiny thump-thump in her chest, as if the model had reminded her of a job.

Callum watched, and the idea arrived the way his best workshop ideas arrived: already holding a screwdriver. He thought of the delicate wires for his bird feeder, the tiny springs for his wind-up mouse. Heart as pump. Vessels as rivers that preferred not to flood.

He went back to the workshop, wood-shavings and all, and gathered delicate wires, a polished brass spring, and fine flexible tubing. He laid them out the way he laid out a bird-feeder repair: smallest parts nearest the light. The first spring was too fierce; it would have shouted. He swapped it for a softer coil and tested the pulse against his own wrist until the beats agreed to be neighbours. He worked with the calm of someone who knew that hurry makes sloppy springs. The miniature contraption was a gentle spring-powered nudge, a soft hum, a steady boost, not a parade.

With Dr. Ada’s quiet nod he fitted the device onto Fern, checking the tubes twice because once is how you invent a new problem, and wound the spring. Whirr. Click. The tiny pump began its barely perceptible work. Callum counted ten cycles before he trusted his own hope.

Slowly, like a shy flower deciding on a Tuesday, Fern’s breathing deepened. The sleepy fog lifted. She wriggled her nose, which in hedgehog is as good as a signed letter.

Dr. Ada beamed. “Circulatory system. Heart as pump, blood as the carrier, oxygen as the reason the whole route exists. Your device is giving her system a helping hand. A steadying one. Not a parade.”

Callum felt a warmth that had nothing to do with beakers. Fern nudged his hand with a damp nose.

He did not wait for a lecture about invention being the same as friendship. He logged shallow breaths / clockwork model / spring nudge in the lab book, left the berry where Fern could reach it without drama, and let Dr. Ada put the teacup-heart back on its stand still ticking. Fern, already looking toward the next berry-picking, had a pulse you could trust. Callum wound the spring one extra click for luck, then stopped himself, because luck is not an engineering specification and Fern had already begun looking for a second berry.
